title: Crème brûlée
summary: A rich vanilla cream custard baked gently in a water bath and finished with a thin, crackly layer of torched allulose.
steps: Heat the oven to 150 °C (300 °F). Set six 120 ml (4 oz) ramekins in a roasting tin.
Heat the cream with the vanilla and salt until steaming, but not boiling.
Whisk the yolks and erythritol until smooth. Pour in the hot cream in a thin stream, whisking gently so you do not beat in air. Strain into a jug.
Divide among the ramekins. Pour hot water into the tin to come halfway up the ramekins.
Bake 30–40 minutes, until the edges are set and the centres wobble like jelly. Lift out of the water, cool, then refrigerate at least 4 hours.
Just before serving, blot any moisture off the tops, sprinkle each evenly with allulose and torch until amber. Let it harden for a minute.
dairy_free_notes: Coconut cream sets a little softer and tastes of coconut; add a pinch more salt and an extra yolk if you want a firmer set.
tips: Allulose caramelises fast and burns fast; keep the torch moving and stop at amber.
Erythritol will not melt into a proper crust, which is why the topping uses allulose.

origin.history: Where crème brûlée began is disputed. A burnt-cream recipe under the French name appears in a cookbook by the French chef François Massialot at the end of the 1600s, while England claims a 'burnt cream' long associated with Trinity College, Cambridge, and Catalonia has its own crema catalana. The dessert became a restaurant standard worldwide in the 1980s.
